I've been farming this land in Quzhou County my whole life. The soil here is good, and the weather pattern is familiar to me — hot, rainy summers and cold, dry winters. Around here, if you have irrigated land, you plant winter wheat in the fall and then summer maize right after the wheat comes off in early June. That's what my family has always done, and it's what the grain buyers expect. I don't have any schooling, but I know this land. I've watched my parents do it, and I've done it myself for over forty years.

This year, I will stick to the wheat–maize rotation on my 6 *mu* of good flat land. I thought about planting vegetables because the prices look tempting sometimes, but vegetables need more labor, closer watching, and a reliable buyer. At my age, I don't have the strength to carry heavy water buckets every day or chase after merchants. Grain is safer — the cooperative buys it, and I can store it if the price is low. I will use the improved wheat seeds and hybrid maize seeds that the county agri-station recommends; they cost a bit more, but they yield better and resist diseases better than the old varieties my grandmother saved.

For the wheat, I will rotary-till the field after the maize stalks are chopped and spread, then plant in mid-October. I will apply fertilizer — more nitrogen than phosphorus or potassium, because that's what the soil here seems to need — and irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings survive the cold, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, and once during grain filling so the grains are plump. I'll spray pesticides twice if I see aphids or rust.

For the maize, I'll plant immediately after wheat harvest in early June. I'll till again with the rotary tiller, broadcast the fertilizer, and irrigate once or twice, mainly around the tasseling stage if the rains don't come. One or two pesticide sprays should be enough for the borers and armyworms that sometimes show up in July and August.

I don't write things down, but I keep the plan in my head: wheat first, maize second, don't waste water, and don't let the weeds win.
